title: Institutional ownership of single-family rentals grew in selected metros without becoming most single-family housing
source_unit: GAO-26-108675 review of institutional investor ownership of single-family rental homes
geography: Six selected U.S. metropolitan statistical areas: Cincinnati, Dallas, Jacksonville, Nashville, Phoenix, and Seattle; 2018-2024

denominator.unit: selected metropolitan statistical areas; nongeneralizable sample

institutional_holdings.value: the number of single-family rental homes owned by institutional investors increased in all six selected metro areas

share_of_all_single_family_homes.value: less than 1% to 3% by 2024 across the six metros
share_of_all_single_family_homes.unit: institutionally owned share of all single-family homes

share_of_single_family_rentals.value: 4% in Seattle to 22% in Jacksonville by 2024
share_of_single_family_rentals.unit: institutionally owned share of single-family rental homes

ownership_pathways.value: investors acquired homes from owner-occupants, other non-owner-occupants, and new construction; in Nashville, 35% came from owner-occupants and 15% were newly constructed by 2024

portfolio_sales.value: sales to others, including owner-occupants, never exceeded 8% of institutional holdings in any year in any selected metro

tenant_and_household_outcomes.value: not observed as a common outcome
tenant_and_household_outcomes.unit: missing rent, eviction, repair, quality, tenant stability, homeownership, and neighborhood-change ledger

observations.method: GAO used property-level ownership and mailing-address information from Intercontinental Exchange and affiliates to identify investors owning at least 5,000 single-family homes nationwide and homes in at least five metros, then compared ownership trends with Census ACS market characteristics.
observations.uncertainty: The six-metro sample was selected for geographic diversity and estimated concentration and is not generalizable to all U.S. markets. The institutional-investor definition excludes smaller or less geographically dispersed owners. Ownership counts do not identify landlord conduct, tenant experience, affordability, or causal housing-market effects.
observations.subgroup: Institutional investors and single-family homes in the six selected metros; acquisition source, rental versus all-single-family denominator, and metro housing structures differ by place.
observations.counterinterpretation: Institutional ownership can increase while remaining a small share of all single-family homes, and bulk purchases may have stabilized housing after the financial crisis or added rental supply. A higher share of the rental subset does not by itself establish monopoly, higher rents, worse maintenance, displacement, or reduced homeownership.

related_sources.claim: GAO official report page and full-report link provide the ownership definitions, six-metro scope, 2018-2024 trends, and denominator ranges.

boundary: This record measures institutional ownership trends in a selected six-metro sample. It does not estimate national ownership, landlord behavior, tenant welfare, rent causation, displacement, homeownership access, or durable neighborhood change.
